note.subject: maths

given: Nothing for this topic. The Higher sheet carries the prism, the trapezium, the sphere, the cone, the quadratic formula, the sine and cosine rules and ½ab sin C, and nothing else.
mustKnow: Rate of change at a point = gradient of the tangent drawn at that point
Average rate over an interval = gradient of the chord joining its two ends
Gradient = rise ÷ run, both read from the axes, never counted in squares
Units of a rate = unit of the vertical axis ÷ unit of the horizontal axis
A negative gradient means the quantity is falling; on a velocity-time graph that is deceleration

notOnThisSpec: Differentiation: the gradient is estimated from a drawn tangent, never calculated from a derivative
Area under a curve, and distance from a velocity-time graph
Rates of change of anything that is not shown as a graph

mustBeAbleTo: Draw a tangent to a curve at a stated point, with a ruler and long enough to read from
Find its gradient from two well-separated points, using the axis scales rather than counting squares
Give the answer with the units the axes imply, and with the right sign
Find an average rate of change as the gradient of a chord between two points on the curve
Explain the difference between an average rate and a rate at an instant, and say which is larger for a curve that steepens
Interpret the gradient of a distance-time graph as speed and of a velocity-time graph as acceleration
Read values and times from a growth or decay curve to the accuracy the grid allows
Say what a gradient means in the words of the context: cooling so many degrees each minute, slowing by so many metres per second each second
sheet.howExamined: M8 Paper 2 (calculator, 75 minutes, 50 marks) carries this almost every series, and Paper 1 can carry the interpretation half. The usual shape is a graph question worth 6-8 marks: draw the curve from a formula (3), read a value or a time from it (1), then 'by drawing a suitable line, estimate the rate ...' (2). Summer 2024 Paper 2 Q9 ran exactly that way, and Summer 2023 Paper 2 Q11 the same with a decay curve. November 2024 Paper 2 Q10 added an interpretation part: say what the gradient means. Schemes run MA1 for the table, MA1 MA1 for plotting and the curve, MA1 for a reading, then MA1 (tangent drawn) MA1 (value from the drawn tangent), with a generous band on the value.
traps: Not drawing a tangent at all, and reading the value of the curve instead of its gradient (Summer 2024 Paper 2 Q9, Summer 2023 Paper 2 Q11)
Using a chord between two points on the curve, which gives an average rather than an instantaneous rate
Counting squares for rise and run without converting to the units on the axes (Summer 2023 Paper 2 Q11, where the scale made the whole question harder)
Taking two points that are close together, so a half-square slip changes the gradient badly
Dropping the minus sign on a falling curve, which turns cooling into warming and braking into acceleration
Giving a bare number with no units when the part asks what the gradient means (November 2024 Paper 2 Q10)
Plotting the starting value wrongly on an exponential curve: at t = 0 the multiplier is 1, not 0 (Summer 2024 Paper 2 Q9)
Computing the rate from the formula when the part says to use the graph

noteBlocks.lede: A straight line has one gradient everywhere. A curve does not, which is what makes it good at describing something that speeds up or slows down: a car pulling away, a cup of tea cooling. The gradient of the tangent at a point is how fast the quantity is changing at that moment.
can: Draw a tangent at a stated point, with a ruler and long enough to read.
Find its gradient from two well-separated points on it.
Give the answer with the units the axes imply, and the right sign.

noteBlocks.text: How fast is it changing right now?

noteBlocks.md: Speed on a distance-time graph is the gradient, and on a straight line you read it once and you are done. Curves are the honest picture of most things: a kettle cools quickly at first and then slowly, so the gradient is different at every point. To get the rate at one moment you lay a ruler along the curve there and measure that line instead.

noteBlocks.alt: The distance-time curve with both a dashed chord from t = 0 to t = 10 and a dashed tangent touching the curve at t = 6 seconds.
noteBlocks.caption: A sledge: the chord gives the average speed of 2.5 m/s over 10 s, the tangent gives about 3 m/s at the instant t = 6 s.

noteBlocks.prompt: What is the name of the straight line that touches a curve at one point and runs along it there?
noteBlocks.explain: A tangent. Its gradient is the curve's gradient at that point, and drawing it is the single step that separates the top answers from the rest.

noteBlocks.md:
Two different questions, two different lines.
**Average rate over an interval** — join the two ends with a straight **chord** and find its gradient. Total change divided by total time.

noteBlocks.prompt: You are running out of time on a 2-mark 'estimate the rate' part. What is worth doing first?
options: Draw the tangent at the right point
Write down the value of the curve there
Write 'increasing'
noteBlocks.answer: Draw the tangent at the right point
noteBlocks.explain: The first of the two marks is for a tangent drawn at the stated point. It costs one ruler line, and it is the mark most candidates never collect.

noteBlocks.md:
**Rate at one instant** — draw the **tangent** at that point and find its gradient.
On a curve that bends, these give different answers, and the wording of the question tells you which one is wanted: 'over the first 4 minutes' means a chord, 'when $t = 4$' means a tangent.

noteBlocks.prompt: A part asks for the rate of cooling **when** $t = 4$ minutes. Which line do you draw?
options: A tangent at $t = 4$
A chord from $t = 0$ to $t = 4$
A vertical line at $t = 4$
noteBlocks.explain: 'When' names one moment. A chord would average the rate across four minutes, and the tea cools far faster at the start than at the end.

noteBlocks.md: **Drawing the tangent well.** Mark the point of contact first. Lay the ruler so the line runs along the curve there — touching, not cutting — and draw it **long**, well past the point on both sides. Length matters because the gradient comes from two points on the line, and the further apart they are, the less a small reading slip costs you.

noteBlocks.prompt: Why draw the tangent long rather than short?
options: So the two points you read from it are far apart and the gradient is more accurate
So it reaches the axes
Because short tangents are not allowed
noteBlocks.answer: So the two points you read from it are far apart and the gradient is more accurate
noteBlocks.explain: A half-square error in reading a point barely matters over a run of eight units, and matters a great deal over a run of one.

noteBlocks.title: Instantaneous rate of change
noteBlocks.why: The tangent method from start to finish. Watch how the two points are chosen and how the axis scales turn into the units of the answer.

noteBlocks.prompt: A tangent passes through $(3, 0)$ and $(9, 18)$ on a distance-time graph. What is its gradient?
noteBlocks.explain: Rise $= 18 - 0 = 18$ and run $= 9 - 3 = 6$, so the gradient is $18 \div 6 = 3$. The units come next.

noteBlocks.md: **The units come off the axes**: the unit going up, divided by the unit going across. Distance in metres against time in seconds gives m/s, which is a speed. Velocity in m/s against seconds gives m/s per second, written m/s², which is an acceleration. Temperature in °C against minutes gives °C per minute. Read the axis labels and the units write themselves.

noteBlocks.prompt: A graph has area in m² up the side and time in weeks along the bottom. What are the units of the gradient?
options: m² per week
m²
weeks per m²
noteBlocks.explain: Vertical unit over horizontal unit. Turning it upside down is a common slip and it changes the meaning completely.

noteBlocks.md: **The sign is information.** A tangent sloping downwards has a negative gradient, and that minus sign is the part of the answer that says *cooling*, *decaying*, *slowing down*. Writing $-5.5$ °C per minute and writing 'cooling at 5.5 °C per minute' both carry it. Writing $5.5$ on its own does not, and an examiner reads it as warming up.

noteBlocks.alt: The same cooling curve with a dashed straight tangent drawn touching it at t = 4 minutes.
noteBlocks.caption: A mug of tea cooling: the tangent at t = 4 minutes has gradient about -5.5 °C per minute.

noteBlocks.prompt: The tangent to the cooling curve at $t = 4$ has gradient about $-5.5$. What does that mean?
options: The tea is cooling by about 5.5 °C every minute at that moment
The tea is at 5.5 °C
The tea has cooled by 5.5 °C altogether
noteBlocks.answer: The tea is cooling by about 5.5 °C every minute at that moment
noteBlocks.explain: A gradient is a rate: how much the vertical quantity changes for each unit of the horizontal one. The minus sign makes it a fall rather than a rise.

noteBlocks.title: Summer 2024 Paper 2 Q9
noteBlocks.md: Candidates drew an exponential graph, read when the starting value had trebled, then had to estimate an instantaneous rate. The majority drew the graph — the value at $x = 0$ was the common loss — and a majority read it correctly. Only the stronger candidates thought to draw a tangent for the last part, and not all of those could work out its gradient. Two marks, and the first of them is for the tangent alone.

noteBlocks.prompt: For a curve $A = 4(1.5)^t$, what is $A$ when $t = 0$?
noteBlocks.explain: $1.5^0 = 1$, so $A = 4 \times 1 = 4$. Plotting that point at zero instead was the common loss in Summer 2024.

noteBlocks.md: Counting squares only works when one square is one unit on **both** axes, and on these graphs it almost never is. If a small square is 0.2 seconds across and 1 metre up, a tangent rising 5 squares over 4 squares has risen 5 m in 0.8 s — a gradient of 6.25 m/s, not 1.25. Convert the squares into the units printed on the axes first, then divide. In Summer 2023 the examiners singled out an awkward grid scale as what made the whole question hard.

noteBlocks.prompt: One small square is 0.2 s across and 1 m up. A tangent rises 4 squares over a run of 5 squares. What is its gradient, in m/s?
noteBlocks.explain: Rise $= 4$ m, run $= 5 \times 0.2 = 1$ s, so the gradient is $4 \div 1 = 4$ m/s. Counting squares alone would have given $0.8$.

noteBlocks.task: Draw a curve that rises steeply and then flattens off. Move the point along it and watch the tangent turn. Find the place where the tangent is horizontal, and the places where it is steepest. Nothing here needs calculus: you are watching the gradient change from point to point, which is the whole idea of this statement.

noteBlocks.title: A ten-second check
noteBlocks.md: Ask whether the size makes sense in the story. A sledge a few seconds into a slope is not moving at 0.6 m/s; tea in a warm room does not cool at 50 °C a minute. A rate that is out by a factor of five is nearly always the scale trap, and a rate with the wrong sign is nearly always a dropped minus.

noteBlocks.prompt: In the sim, what is true at the point where the tangent lies flat?
options: The rate of change is zero there
The quantity is zero there
The curve stops there
noteBlocks.answer: The rate of change is zero there
noteBlocks.explain: A horizontal tangent has gradient zero, so at that instant the quantity is momentarily not changing — the top of a hill or the bottom of a dip.

noteBlocks.md:
Tell a chord from a tangent, and draw the tangent long.
Find its gradient from two well-separated points on it.
Read the units off the two axes.
Say what a negative gradient means in the story.

Two or three marks: draw a tangent at the named point, then work out its gradient with the axis scales. The first mark is the tangent itself, so draw it even when the reading defeats you. The last is the rate with its units. Stuck: draw the tangent and mark two points on it that sit on grid intersections.

workedExamples.stem:
A sledge slides down a slope. The graph shows the distance it has travelled against time.

(a) Work out its average speed over the whole 10 seconds.
(b) Estimate its speed at the instant $t = 6$ s.

figure.alt: The distance-time curve with both a dashed chord from t = 0 to t = 10 and a dashed tangent touching the curve at t = 6 seconds.

steps.working: Average speed $= \dfrac{25 - 0}{10 - 0} = 2.5$ m/s
steps.decision: An average rate is the gradient of the straight chord joining the two ends, because it is total change in distance divided by total change in time. That is the dashed line across the whole curve.

steps.working: Draw a tangent that touches the curve at $t = 6$ and lies along it there.
steps.decision: The speed at one instant is not an average over anything, so a chord will not do. The straight line that matches the curve's direction at that single point is the tangent, and its gradient is the instantaneous rate.

options: Because the tangent has the same direction as the curve at that one point
Because the tangent joins the two ends of the curve
Because every chord is a tangent
whyMenu.explain: A chord measures an average across an interval. A tangent touches at one point, so its gradient is the rate at that instant.

steps.working: Two points on the drawn tangent: $(3, 0)$ and $(9, 18)$.
steps.decision: Pick two points far apart and read them off the axes, not by counting squares. Far-apart points keep the gradient accurate; the axis scales turn squares into seconds and metres.

steps.working: Gradient $= \dfrac{18 - 0}{9 - 3} = 3$
steps.decision: Rise over run, both taken from the axes. This is the number the mark scheme calls the value from the drawn tangent.

steps.working: Speed at $t = 6$ s is about $3$ m/s.
steps.decision: Units come from the axes: metres on the vertical, seconds on the horizontal, so the gradient is metres per second. It is larger than the average of $2.5$ m/s because the sledge is still speeding up.

twin.stem: Using the same graph, estimate the sledge's average speed between $t = 4$ s and $t = 8$ s.

workedExamples.stem:
A mug of tea cools in a room. Its temperature $T$ °C after $t$ minutes is shown on the graph.

By drawing a suitable line, estimate the rate at which the tea is cooling when $t = 4$ minutes.

Give the units of your answer.

figure.alt: The same cooling curve with a dashed straight tangent drawn touching it at t = 4 minutes.

steps.working: At $t = 4$ the curve is at about $T = 39$ °C.
steps.decision: Find the point of contact first and mark it. A tangent drawn at the wrong place answers a different question.

steps.working: Lay a ruler along the curve at that point and draw a long straight line touching it there.
steps.decision: Long, because the gradient is read from two points on the line and they should be far apart. Touching, because a line that cuts through the curve is a chord and measures an average instead.

options: Because a long tangent lets you use two widely separated points, which makes the gradient more accurate
Because the tangent must reach the axes
Because a short tangent is not allowed
whyMenu.explain: A small error in reading a point matters far less when the two points are far apart, so a long tangent gives a more reliable gradient.

steps.working: Two points on the tangent: $(1, 55.4)$ and $(7, 22.6)$.
steps.decision: Both read from the axes. The vertical axis is in degrees and the horizontal in minutes, which is where the units of the answer come from.
Rise over run. The rise is negative because the temperature is falling as time goes forward.

steps.working: The tea is cooling at about $5.5$ °C per minute.
steps.decision: The sign is information, not decoration: negative means falling. Saying 'cooling at 5.5 °C per minute' or 'the rate of change is −5.5 °C per minute' both carry it; a bare number with no units carries nothing.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: About $-5.5$ °C per minute (accept -6.17 to -4.75), i.e. the tea is cooling at about $5.5$ °C each minute

twin.stem: Using the same cooling graph, estimate the average rate of change of temperature over the first 4 minutes.

workedExamples.stem:
A tram brakes as it approaches a stop. The graph shows its velocity against time.

Estimate its acceleration at $t = 5$ s, and say what your answer means.

figure.alt: A velocity-time graph for a tram: a curve from 30 m/s at t = 0 to 0 m/s at t = 10 s, with a dashed tangent meeting it at t = 5 seconds.

steps.working: Contact point: at $t = 5$ the velocity is $22.5$ m/s.
steps.decision: Mark the point before drawing anything, so the tangent touches in the right place.

steps.working: Draw the tangent at that point with a ruler, extending it well either side.
steps.decision: On a velocity-time graph the gradient is the rate at which velocity changes, which is acceleration. Nothing else on the diagram measures that.
Rise over run again, with the rise negative because the tangent slopes downwards.

steps.working: Acceleration is about $-3$ m/s².
steps.decision: The units are the vertical unit divided by the horizontal unit: metres per second, per second. That is written m/s², and it is worth a mark of its own in an interpretation part.

options: Because the vertical axis is m/s and the horizontal is s, so the gradient is m/s per s
Because acceleration is always measured in m/s
Because the units come from the equation of the curve
whyMenu.explain: Every gradient carries the unit of the vertical axis divided by the unit of the horizontal axis. Read them off the axis labels and the units follow.

steps.working: The velocity is falling by about $3$ m/s every second at that moment: the tram is slowing down.
steps.decision: The November 2024 examiners reported that the part asking what a gradient means was answered by only just over half the entry. A sentence naming the quantity, the size and the direction is what earns it.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: About $-3$ m/s² (accept -3.39 to -2.61): the tram is slowing down by roughly $3$ m/s each second

twin.stem: Using the same velocity-time graph, estimate the tram's acceleration at $t = 8$ s.

workedExamples.stem:
Duckweed spreads across a pond. Its area $A$ m² after $t$ weeks is shown on the graph.

(a) Estimate the average rate at which the area grew over the first 4 weeks.
(b) Estimate the rate at which it was growing at the instant $t = 4$ weeks.
(c) Explain why the two answers differ.

figure.alt: The same growth curve with a dashed straight tangent drawn touching it at t = 4 weeks.

steps.working: Average rate $= \dfrac{20.25 - 4}{4 - 0} = 4.06$ m² per week
steps.decision: Average over an interval means the gradient of the chord: change in area divided by change in time, both read off the axes.

steps.working: Draw the tangent at $t = 4$ with a ruler.
steps.decision: For the rate at an instant the chord is no use, because the growth is speeding up all the way along. Only a tangent measures the rate at one moment.

steps.working: Two points on the tangent: $(2, 3.8)$ and $(6, 36.7)$. Gradient $= \dfrac{36.7 - 3.8}{6 - 2} = 8.2$
steps.decision: Rise over run from the axes, the points chosen four weeks apart so the reading is stable.

steps.working: About $8.2$ m² per week.
steps.decision: Area on the vertical axis and weeks on the horizontal, so the units are square metres per week.

steps.working: $8.2 > 4.06$, because the curve is getting steeper.
steps.decision: The average is spread over four weeks that include the slow start; the instantaneous rate is measured at the end, where the curve is steepest. On any curve that bends upwards the final instantaneous rate beats the average.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: (a) $4.06$ m² per week  (b) about $8.2$ m² per week (accept 7.14 to 9.28)  (c) the growth is speeding up, so the rate at the end of the interval is greater than the average across it

findTheMistake.stem: Méabh drew a correct tangent on a distance-time graph and then found its gradient. One small square is 0.2 seconds across and 1 metre up. Her working:
studentWorking: It rises 18 small squares and runs across 30 small squares
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 3 divides squares by squares. The two axes are not on the same scale: 18 squares up is $18$ m, but 30 squares across is only $6$ s. Ignoring that makes the answer five times too small, and $0.6$ m/s for a sledge already several seconds into a slope should have looked wrong.
findTheMistake.feedback: Drawing the tangent is the step most candidates never reach, and it carries the method mark, so the hard part is already done. Convert squares into the units on the axes before dividing, and check the answer against the context: a sledge on a slope is not moving at half a metre per second by then.

findTheMistake.stem: Asked what the gradient of a velocity-time graph tells you at $t = 5$ s, Ruairí wrote:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 2 drops the minus sign. The tangent slopes downwards, so the gradient is $-3$, not $3$. That sign is the difference between a tram that is braking and one that is speeding up, and line 3 then describes the wrong motion. The units are missing as well.
correction: The velocity is falling by about 3 m/s every second
So the tram is slowing down, not accelerating
findTheMistake.feedback: The tangent and the size of the gradient are both right, and they earn the method mark. Read the direction of the line before you write the number, and finish with the units: the November 2024 examiners reported that the part asking what a gradient means was answered by only just over half the entry.

prompts.prompt: How do you estimate the rate of change of a curve at a given point?
prompts.answer: Draw a tangent touching the curve at that point with a ruler, take two points on the tangent that are far apart, read both from the axes, and work out rise ÷ run.

prompts.prompt: What is the difference between an average rate of change and an instantaneous one?
prompts.answer: The average rate over an interval is the gradient of the chord joining its two ends. The instantaneous rate at a point is the gradient of the tangent there.

prompts.prompt: Where do the units of a rate read from a graph come from?
prompts.answer: The unit of the vertical axis divided by the unit of the horizontal axis: metres and seconds give m/s; degrees and minutes give °C per minute.

prompts.prompt: What does the gradient of a distance-time graph measure, and in what units?
prompts.answer: Speed, in units of distance per unit of time, for example metres per second.

prompts.prompt: What does the gradient of a velocity-time graph measure, and in what units?
prompts.answer: Acceleration, in m/s per second, written m/s².

prompts.prompt: Why must the two points you use come from the tangent and not from the curve?
prompts.answer: Two points on the curve define a chord, and a chord measures the average rate across the gap between them. Only the tangent has the curve's direction at the single point.

prompts.prompt: The tangent slopes downwards. What must the answer include?
prompts.answer: The minus sign. A negative gradient means the quantity is falling: cooling, decaying, slowing down. Dropping it describes the opposite behaviour.

prompts.prompt: One small square is 0.2 s across and 1 m up. Why can you not just count squares?
prompts.answer: The scales differ, so the same number of squares means different amounts on the two axes. Convert to seconds and metres first, then divide.

prompts.prompt: A tangent passes through (3, 0) and (9, 18) on a distance-time graph in metres and seconds. What is the speed there?
A curve gets steeper as it goes. How does the instantaneous rate at the end of an interval compare with the average rate across it?
prompts.answer: It is larger. The average includes the flatter start, while the instantaneous rate is measured where the curve is steepest.

findings.asked: Sketch a decay curve over four years, read a value from it, then find the rate of decay at a stated time.
findings.wentWrong: The chosen scale made a smooth curve hard to draw and markers were generous; the curve and the reading both scored acceptably. The tangent for the rate of decay was completed only by the best candidates.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Drew the tangent with a ruler at the stated time and took two well-separated points off the axes to find its gradient.
findings.rule: A rate of change at a stated moment is the gradient of the tangent drawn there.

findings.asked: Draw an exponential growth graph, read when the starting value had trebled, then estimate the instantaneous rate of increase at a stated value of x.
findings.wentWrong: The majority drew the graph, with the value at x = 0 the common loss, and a majority read it correctly. Only the stronger candidates thought to draw a tangent, and not all of those could find its gradient.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Plotted the starting value correctly, then drew a long tangent and used two distant points on it with the axis scales.
findings.rule: Draw the tangent with a ruler, pick two far-apart points on it, and use the scales.

findings.asked: Draw a curve, use it, and interpret what a gradient means.
findings.wentWrong: The curves were generally good. The part that used the curve was answered by fewer than half, and the part asking what the gradient meant by just over half.
findings.rule: Say what the gradient measures, in the units of the axes, and in the language of the context.

insight.ruleToRemember: The gradient at a point on a curve is the gradient of the tangent drawn there; draw it with a ruler, use two distant points and the axis scales, and interpret it with units and a sign.
insight.aStarSignal: Drawing a tangent unprompted and turning its gradient into a rate with units and a direction.
